request: Kinetic energy: where the ½mv² comes from #interactive

elements.details: With calculus the same steps hold for ANY force, steady or not: $$W=\int F\,dx=\int m\frac{dv}{dt}\,dx=\int_0^v m\,v\,dv=\tfrac12 mv^2$$

commands.speak: Where does kinetic energy's one-half m v squared come from, and why should a driver care? Start with a car that brakes from 50 kilometres an hour to a stop in about 14 metres.

ask.question: Same car, same brakes, but at 100 kilometres an hour. How many metres to stop? Click your guess.
ask.right: You said {g} metres, and it is about {g.true}: twice the speed, four times the road. Hold on to that.
ask.wrong: You said {g} metres; it is about {g.true}, {g.off} off. A very common guess is 28, simply double. It is four times, and one-half m v squared says why.

commands.speak: To see why, build the energy of motion from scratch: it is the work it takes to get the car moving.
Work is a force times the distance it pushes through.
So push: a 1000-kilogram car, from rest, with a steady 2000 newtons.
A steady force gives a steady gain: two metres per second faster, every second. After five seconds, ten metres per second.
How far has it gone? At ten metres per second the whole time, it would cover this rectangle: ten times five, fifty metres.
But it was not doing ten the whole time. So the distance is only some share of v times t.

ask.question: Which tile finishes the distance?
ask.right: One half: the speed climbs evenly from zero to v, so on average it is only v over two.
ask.wrong: Think of the speed halfway through the push.

commands.speak: That is the triangle under the speed line: twenty-five metres, exactly half the rectangle.
Now the force: mass times acceleration, and acceleration is the speed gained, v, over the time it took, t.
Put in the distance: one half of v times t.
The times cancel, and out comes one-half m v squared.
So the half is the triangle: anything speeding up from rest only ever averages half its final speed.
Check it on the car: 2000 newtons over 25 metres is 50,000 joules.
And one half times 1000 times ten squared: 50,000 again.
The force itself has dropped out: a gentler push takes longer and goes further, and the work comes to the same.
That v squared was once hotly disputed. Émilie du Châtelet argued for it in 1740: balls dropped into soft clay at twice the speed sank four times as deep.
The half came about a century later, when engineers like Gaspard Coriolis defined work as force times distance.

quiz.question: Which costs more work: speeding up from 0 to 10 m/s, or from 10 to 20 m/s?
quiz.right: From 10 to 20 costs three times as much: already moving fast, each second of pushing covers far more road, so the triangle underneath is much bigger.
quiz.wrong: Same gain in speed, but is it the same distance pushed?

commands.speak: See it directly: push for ten seconds instead of five. Twice the time, twice the top speed…
…and four times the triangle: a hundred metres, so 200 kilojoules instead of 50. Twice as long, at twice the average speed.
Braking runs the same film backwards. The brakes' force is fixed, so four times the energy needs four times the road: 14 metres becomes about 55. You guessed {g}.
So one-half m v squared is just force times distance: the square is speed counted twice, and the half is a triangle.

quiz.question: A car speeds up from 30 to 90 kilometres an hour. Its kinetic energy…
quiz.right: Nine times: energy goes with speed squared, and three squared is nine, so it needs nine times the road to brake.
quiz.wrong: Remember what doubling the speed did to the triangle.
